Rev. '''Hamnet Holditch''', also spelled '''Hamnett Holditch''' (1800 – 12 December 1867), was an English mathematician who was President of [[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge]]. In 1858, he introduced the result in [[geometry]] now known as [[Holditch's theorem]].

Hamnet Holditch was born in 1800 in [[King's Lynn]], the son of George Holditch, [[maritime pilot|pilot]] and harbour-master. Educated at King's Lynn Grammar School under Rev. Martin Coulcher,<ref name="Hillen">{{cite book|last=Hillen|first=Henry J.|title=Biographical History of the Borough of King's Lynn|volume=2|page=632|year=1907|url=https://archive.org/details/historyofborough02hill/page/632|access-date=1 January 2022}}</ref> he matriculated at [[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge]] in 1818, and graduated [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] in 1822 ([[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Senior Wrangler]] and 1st [[Smith's Prize]]), [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)|M.A.]] in 1825.<ref name="acad-venn">{{acad|id=HLDC818H|name=Holditch, Hamnett}}</ref>

At Gonville and Caius College, Holditch was a junior fellow from 1821 and a senior fellow from 1823, and held the college posts of lecturer in Hebrew and Greek, registrar, steward, salarist (1823–28), bursar (1828–31), and President (1835–67).<ref name="Venn"/><ref>David Taylor, [http://www.holdiches.com/2013/06/reverend-hamnett-holditch-1800-1867/ "Reverend Hamnett Holditch (1800–1867)"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141016041202/http://www.holdiches.com/2013/06/reverend-hamnett-holditch-1800-1867/ |date=2014-10-16 }}, ''HFHS Journal'', Issue 24 (May 2003).</ref>

He died at Gonville and Caius College on 12 December 1867, aged 67,<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Urban|first=Sylvanus|magazine=The Gentleman's Magazine and Historical Review|year=1868|volume=5|page=255|title=Deaths|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m5tQAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA255|access-date=1 January 2022}}</ref> and was buried at [[North Wootton, Norfolk|North Wootton]].<ref name="Hillen"/><ref name="Venn"/>

Although Holditch produced ten mathematical papers, he was extremely idle as a tutor.<ref>{{cite book|last=Craik|first=A. D. D.|year=2007|title=Mr Hopkins' Men: Cambridge reform and British mathematics in the 19th century|page=44|publisher=Springer|isbn=9781846287916|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=te4t81kg1JQC&pg=PA44|access-date=24 December 2021}}</ref> [[John Venn]], an undergraduate at Caius in the 1850s then a Caius Fellow from 1857, noted that Holditch, despite his succession of college offices, "beyond a few private pupils, never took part in educational work":<ref name="Venn"/>

{{Blockquote|text=He was a very ingenious mathematician, and would probably have distinguished himself had he been compelled to work. Remarkable for his extreme shyness. On account of some ancient slight he for many years entirely absented himself from Hall and Chapel, and few members of the college knew him even by sight:— an undergraduate once showed him round the college, taking him for a stranger. The whole summer he spent fishing in Scotland or Wales.|author=[[John Venn]]|title=''Biographical History of Gonville and Caius College''<ref name="Venn">{{cite book|last=Venn|first=John|title=Biographical History of Gonville and Caius College|volume=2|page=170|year=1898|publisher=CUP Archive|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pNs8AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA170|access-date=1 January 2022}}</ref>}}

{{Blockquote|text=It is curious to see Holditch coming out of his den, which he does once in ten years, with something about rolling curves or caustics. He was senior wrangler the year before [[George Biddell Airy|Airy]], and what has made a man of such decided talent shut himself up I never heard.|author=[[Augustus De Morgan]] (1865)<ref>{{cite journal|last=Crilly|first=Tony|year=2004|title=The ''Cambridge Mathematical Journal'' and its descendants: the linchpin of a research community in the early and mid-Victorian Age|journal=Historia Mathematica|volume=31|issue=4|page=488|doi=10.1016/j.hm.2004.03.001|doi-access=}}</ref>}}
